# A restored pod's captured address

Status: built, behind `agent.restoreCapturedAddress` (default off); section 7 lists what is not built. Scope: `internal/agent/restore_address.go`
(`planCapturedAddress`, `capturedAddressRules`, `restoreCapturedAddress`, `restoreSourceAddress`,
`inetAddrMapKeeping`), `instance_nat.go`, `restore.go` (single-pod alias), `restore_v2.go` (group restore),
`pidns_capture.go` (CRIU restore arguments).

## 1. Problem

A restored pod has a new pod IP, but its processes remember the captured pod's IP. CRIU moves the sockets that exist
at the dump (through the inet address map for a group restore, or by keeping the old address on the placeholder's
loopback for a single pod); a socket created after the restore is not covered.

NCCL opens peer connections lazily, on first use, and binds the listener to the interface address it read at
startup: the captured IP. The bind fails (`Call to bind failed: Cannot assign requested address`, then
`Rank 0 has no transport for send peer 7`), and the engine dies on its first requests. With 2 ranks every connection
opens during warm-up, before the capture; at tens of ranks some pairs connect only after the restore.

## 2. Requirements

1. A socket bound to the captured address after the restore can listen and connect.
2. Peers that learned the captured address (NCCL's handles, an engine's advertised address) reach it.
3. Restored sockets keep working, including established connections conntrack picks up mid-stream.
4. IP reuse is safe. Pod IPs are recycled (the AWS VPC CNI reuses a freed IP quickly, often for the next pod of the
   same function), so the captured IP may belong, now or later, to another member of the instance or an unrelated
   pod. A restored pod must neither capture that pod's traffic nor lose the ability to talk to it.
5. Idempotent, IPv4 and IPv6, no change to the workload; kubelet probes, Services and clients outside the instance
   unaffected.

## 3. IP reuse: what a local captured IP exposes

A local captured IP (the loopback alias) satisfies 1 to 3 but not 4:

- If it is another member's new IP, the alias delivers that member's traffic locally.
- If it is (or becomes) an unrelated pod's IP, packets that pod sends straight to the restored pod's IP arrive with a
  local source and are dropped. Traffic through a Service is not affected: the node rewrites the backend's address to
  the Service's on the way back.

A socket can use the captured IP only if it is a local address, so this exposure cannot be removed without the
workload's cooperation; it can only be detected and bounded (section 5).

## 4. Options tested (GB300, AWS VPC CNI, kube-proxy iptables, 2026-10-25)

| | How | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A. Captured IP on `lo` + edge NAT | captured IP local on `lo`; SNAT it to the pod IP on the way out; DNAT unclaimed inbound to it | works: binds, listens and connects from the captured IP; probes and Services unaffected. Exposed to IP reuse (section 3) |
| B. Non-local bind + marked local delivery | `ip_nonlocal_bind`, DNAT unclaimed SYNs to the captured IP, deliver by fwmark route | fails: the kernel does not route a socket's packets from a non-local address (no `IP_TRANSPARENT` on application sockets), so SYN-ACKs and outbound connects get `ENETUNREACH` |
| C. Keep every captured address inside the pod | drop CRIU's address rewrite; NAT every member address both ways | same exposure as A, Service-alias flows break when the peer speaks first, and a large change to a working path |

## 5. A with reuse guards

In the restored pod's network namespace, before its tasks run (before CRIU for a single pod, before the network
unlock for a group), and only when the pod IP changed (`planCapturedAddress` decides, `capturedAddressRules` builds):

- `ip addr add <captured>/32 dev lo` (`/128` for IPv6).
- `nat POSTROUTING -s <captured> ! -o lo -j SNAT --to-source <pod IP>`: traffic leaving the pod carries the pod IP;
  traffic over the loopback (the pod's connections to its own captured address, such as NCCL's to its proxy) keeps the
  captured address at both ends.
- `mangle PREROUTING -d <pod IP> -p tcp -m socket --nowildcard -j MARK`, then
  `nat PREROUTING -d <pod IP> -p tcp -m mark ! --mark <claim> -j DNAT --to-destination <captured>`: a packet a socket
  bound to the pod IP or the wildcard accepts keeps its destination (the engine's API, a probe); any other goes to the
  captured address. Not limited to SYNs, because a restored connection's first packet after the restore can come from
  its peer and the nat table sees only a connection's first packet (`TestCapturedAddressRules` checks no `--syn` rule).
- The existing DNAT of the instance's other captured addresses stays, with the pod's own entry dropped from the
  address map (`inetAddrMapKeeping`), so its sockets stay on the captured address.

Rules live in nvsnap's own chains (`NVSNAP-RESTORE-*`), flushed and refilled on each attempt, and go away with the
pod's network namespace.

Reuse guards: the alias and rules are skipped, the restore continues without them, and a warning plus the metric
`RestoreCapturedAddressTotal` (`internal/metrics/metrics.go`) record why, when the captured IP is the new IP of a member of the restored
instance, or the IP of any pod in the cluster at restore time.

Not guaranteed: when a guard skips (or applying fails) and the inet address map does not move the captured address,
the restore falls back to the switch-off behaviour and adds the old unguarded loopback alias, with section 3's
exposure (`internal/agent/restore_address.go` `restoreSourceAddress`; `TestRestoreSourceAddress`).

Not guaranteed: a pod given the captured IP after the restore cannot reach the restored pod by pod IP directly (its
packets arrive with a local source). Service traffic is unaffected. Several instances restored from one capture each
hold the captured address privately, on their own loopback and never advertised, so they do not conflict with each
other.

With the switch off, the single-pod path keeps its old alias, unguarded (section 3's second exposure); with it on, it
gets the same guards, except for the fallback above.

## 6. Verification

- Unit: rule sets for v4, v6 and dual stack; nothing installed when the pod IP did not change; idempotent re-apply;
  the guard for a member's new IP and for an IP held by a pod; CRIU arguments unchanged.
- GB300 conformance: `sts8` (the failure above) passes; `sts2`, `comp1`, `shpid1`, `xnode1`, `xnode2`, `deploy1`
  and `setsid1` unchanged; `sts16` when the nodes are free; a guard case where another pod holds the captured IP.
- A 4-worker Kimi-K3 instance through the scale up/down test.

## 7. Before default on, and later

- `agent.restoreCapturedAddress` turns on by default only after `sts8`, the full conformance suite, a guard test and
  the 4-worker scale test pass, on one cluster first.
- Not built: detection of a later reuse conflict (packets dropped in a restored pod because their source is its
  captured address, logged with the pod).
- The cause is upstream: NCCL binds lazily created listeners to the address it read at startup. Binding them to the
  wildcard, or re-reading the address, would remove the need for the alias.
